articles.title: BepiColombo’s Mercury arrival begins - full replay
articles.description:
Video: 
			02:31:10
				
Watch the replay of the livestream originally broadcast on 3 September as ESA/JAXA's BepiColombo mission took the first critical step towards arriving at Mercury.
After travelling through the inner Solar System together for eight years, BepiColombo's Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from the rest of the stacked spacecraft on 3 September 2026. This marks the beginning of one of the most complex planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.
Broadcast live from ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany, the programme includes live views from the iconic Main Control Room, expert analysis, behind-the-scenes insights, and the first signal from the spacecraft following separation. 
Livestream schedule (CEST): 

13:45 – Livestream begins 
16:00-16:45 – End of livestream
articles.summary: BepiColombo's historic arrival at Mercury is celebrated with a full replay of ESA/JAXA's livestream coverage of this landmark achievement in planetary exploration.

articles.title: NASA's First Selection for a New Class of Mission: The PRIMA Far-Infrared Telescope
articles.description: NASA announced Wednesday a mission to explore the history and evolution of the universe, PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), is advancing to the next phase of development. This space telescope is the first in a new class of NASA astrophysics missions, called Probe Explorers, within the agency’s longstanding Explorers Program.
articles.summary: NASA selects PRIMA, a far-infrared telescope mission designed to explore the history and evolution of the universe. This represents a major advancement in observational cosmology and deep-space exploration capabilities.

articles.title: The phoenix planet: Astronomers find a world reborn from its star's ashes
articles.description: Astronomers have discovered the first example of a second-generation planet orbiting a white dwarf, a world that appears to have formed from the remains of the dead star it now orbits.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers discover the first known second-generation planet orbiting a white dwarf, apparently formed from the stellar remnant's material. This remarkable find reveals unexpected planetary formation possibilities in stellar death scenarios.

articles.title: NASA’s Roman telescope just opened its planet-hunting eye
articles.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has demonstrated remarkable pointing stability and given its powerful planet-imaging coronagraph its first look at the cosmos. The telescope can already stay locked on a target with precision comparable to aiming a laser at a dime from about 150 miles away. Its coronagraph also captured stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, confirming that the instrument can produce focused images.
articles.summary: NASA's Roman Space Telescope demonstrates exceptional pointing stability and activates its powerful planet-hunting coronagraph. This achievement represents a major step forward in direct exoplanet imaging and characterization.

articles.title: First Direct Image of Protoplanet Swirling Surrounding Gas
articles.description: The formation and evolution of planets is the driving force behind both where and how we might find life beyond Earth. This complex and lengthy process first begins with a massive ball of gas and dust that swirls until it flattens into a disk, followed by roc…
articles.summary: Astronomers have captured the first direct image of a protoplanet forming within its surrounding gas disk, advancing our understanding of planetary formation.

articles.title: The Universe Is Full of Tiny Red Dots—and They’re One of Astronomy’s Biggest Discoveries in Decades
articles.description: A new type of object found in the early universe has puzzled astronomers for years, but they may finally have some answers.
articles.summary: Astronomers have identified and begun understanding a new class of mysterious tiny red objects in the early universe, representing a major discovery.

articles.title: NASA 宣布最新遠紅外線望遠鏡 PRIMA 計畫，探索星球形成與材料之謎
articles.description:
恆星如何從厚重的塵埃誕生？行星水又從哪裡來？NASA 宣布新遠紅外線太空望遠鏡 PRIMA（PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics，意為「天文物理遠紅外線探測任務」）獲選進入下階段開發，目標 2033 年發射，展開為期五年觀測。

這項任務源自天文學界 2020 年對未來十年研究方向的整體建議，規模介於小型探索任務與大型旗艦望遠鏡之間，希望補足現有設備的觀測能力。目前 PRIMA 將進行初步設計與技術開發，之後若通過確認審查，專案成本上限為 12 億美元，不含發射…
articles.summary: NASA announces the PRIMA far-infrared space telescope program selected for development, designed to explore star and planet formation by investigating how stars form in dusty environments and the origins of planetary water. This represents a major advancement in astrophysics research capabilities.

articles.title: Science begins for Smile
articles.description: On 23 September, the European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to start revealing how Earth responds to the wind of charged particles from the Sun. This follows a busy in-space commissioning period since the spacecraft launched on 19 May and reached its target orbit for science operations on 20 June.
articles.summary: The European-Chinese Smile mission has been declared ready to begin science operations, studying how Earth's magnetosphere responds to solar wind interactions.

articles.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
articles.description:
Image:
			
This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us.
MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.
The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing, in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity.
The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. The galaxy group appears to be going through a merger, resulting in an enormous burst of star formation.
Astronomers have also identified individual bright ‘knots’ within the gravitationally lensed areas, corresponding to regions as small as 5 light-years across. These tiny clumps appear magnified by a factor of more than 300, in some cases.
A NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of this same cluster was released in 2014. Take a moment to compare the two images; the difference between them is dramatic. The new Webb image reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier image. These galaxies were there all along, but Webb is much more sensitive to their much redder light.
The data behind this image come from two observing programmes (#5058, PI: Furtak; #6882, PI: Fujimoto) that leverage the ability of massive galaxy clusters to bring distant objects into view.
[Image Description: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the centre. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's centre; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in colour; bright, nearby stars are the same colour.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope reveals galaxies in unprecedented detail through a cosmic gravitational lensing effect, showcasing the power of modern space-based observations.

articles.title: New Simulations Connect the First Galaxies to the Universe We See Today
articles.description: In a recent study, researchers at the international MEGATRON project used some of the most detailed simulations of the early Universe to investigate how the first stars and galaxies formed.
articles.summary: The MEGATRON project's detailed simulations connect the formation of the first galaxies to the structure of the modern universe, bridging cosmic history.

articles.title: Chandra X-ray Observatory Drops New View of our Galaxy’s Unruly Centre
articles.description: The core of the Milky Way is a dense, active, messy region, dominated by a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) hiding at the heart of the galaxy. But Sgr A* is only a supporting actor in this stunning new image from the Chandra X-ray Observatory.
articles.summary: The Chandra X-ray Observatory provides a new detailed view of the Milky Way's galactic center, revealing the dynamic environment surrounding Sagittarius A*.

articles.title: Neutrons, Rotating Black Holes, and a Galactic PeVatron at the Center of the Milky Way
articles.description: Supermassive black holes generate tremendous amounts of energy through their accretion disks and jets. But they can also generate energy through the magnetic Penrose process. A new study looks at how we might observe this process through multimessenger astronomy.
articles.summary: Research reveals how supermassive black holes at the galactic center generate tremendous energy and may function as cosmic particle accelerators called PeVatrons.

articles.title: XRISM Makes First-Ever Detection of a Pulsar Feeding from a Companion's Stellar "Wind"
articles.description: Using data from the Japan-led XRISM observatory, astronomers have directly observed a giant star’s stellar wind captured by its compact companion (triggering X-ray flares) for the first time.
articles.summary: The XRISM observatory makes the first direct observation of a pulsar capturing stellar wind from a companion star, revealing new insights into extreme astrophysical systems.

articles.title: Astronomers catch a star slowly snacking on a brown dwarf, 300 light years away
articles.description: Like Earth, most planetary bodies circle their star in stable, detached orbits. These companionable systems can suddenly change when a planet comes too close to its star. In such a close encounter, a star can pull the planet in and swallow it whole.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers observe a star gradually consuming a brown dwarf 300 light-years away, providing rare direct evidence of stellar cannibalism. This discovery illuminates the dynamic interactions possible within binary systems.

articles.title: This mysterious hole on the Moon may open into a giant cave
articles.description: NASA has selected the GIMLI project to investigate whether the Marius Hill Pit opens into a vast underground cave or lava tube. Using radar, seismic sensors, gravity measurements, and cameras, researchers will search beneath the lunar surface and estimate the size of any hidden void. Such caves could preserve clues to the Moon’s volcanic history and potentially provide protected shelters for future astronauts.
articles.summary: NASA selects the GIMLI project to investigate the Marius Hill Pit and determine if it opens into a vast underground lunar cave. This mission promises groundbreaking discoveries about the Moon's subsurface geology.

articles.title: Scientists find a surprising clue to why the universe’s expansion doesn’t add up
articles.description: Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help explain the long-running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding. Detailed simulations show that these primordial fields could have changed the formation of hydrogen in the early universe, affecting the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate inferred from it.
articles.summary: Scientists identify tiny magnetic fields created after the Big Bang as a potential explanation for discrepancies in universe expansion measurements. This breakthrough may resolve a major puzzle in cosmological physics.

articles.title: ESA’s Juice just used Earth as a slingshot to Jupiter
articles.description: ESA’s Juice spacecraft raced past Earth on September 28, using our planet’s gravity to dramatically reshape its path toward Jupiter without burning much fuel. The flyby changed its direction by 20 degrees and increased its speed by 3.5 km/s, while also giving scientists a rare chance to test its instruments on Earth and the Moon.
articles.summary: ESA's Juice spacecraft successfully uses Earth's gravity as a slingshot to reshape its trajectory toward Jupiter. This successful maneuver marks a critical milestone in one of humanity's most ambitious planetary exploration missions.

articles.title: Chang’e-6 lunar soil contains a surprising magnetic time capsule
articles.description: Scientists studying Chang’e-6 lunar soil have discovered a previously unknown magnetic mineral in natural Moon samples: a form of metallic iron called γ-Fe. Found inside tiny impact-glass particles, the nanoscale iron can preserve a stable magnetic signal, potentially acting like a microscopic fossil of the Moon’s long-lost magnetic field.
articles.summary: Analysis of Chang'e-6 lunar samples reveals a previously unknown magnetic mineral, serving as a magnetic time capsule of the Moon's history. This discovery deepens our understanding of lunar geological processes.

articles.title: Powerful simulations reveal how the first stars changed the universe
articles.description: Ultra-detailed simulations are showing how the first stars lit up the dark Universe and seeded space with elements such as carbon, oxygen, and iron. The MEGATRON project could bridge JWST observations of the earliest galaxies with chemical clues preserved in ancient stars today.
articles.summary: Advanced simulations reveal how the first stars illuminated the dark universe and distributed essential elements throughout space. This research profoundly enhances our understanding of cosmic evolution and structure formation.

articles.title: China's FAST telescope to advance with Phase II construction as project marks 10th anniversary
articles.description: The Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST), known as the China's "Sky Eyes", will mark the 10th anniversary of its inauguration on September 25. Since its launch, the facility has achieved a series of landmark scientific and technologica…
articles.summary: China's FAST radio telescope, the world's largest spherical aperture, advances to Phase II construction while celebrating its 10th anniversary.

articles.title: SpaceX's Starship Needs To Be Fully Operational By 2028 — Here's Why
articles.description: SpaceX has plenty left to test on Starship, from refueling to docking in orbit, and NASA is counting on it to finish in time for a much bigger assignment.
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship must reach full operational capability by 2028 to support NASA's lunar mission timeline, with critical testing phases remaining.

articles.title: New space race: Superpowers look to set up N-reactors on the Moon
articles.description: The US, China and Russia are racing to deploy nuclear reactors on the Moon, seeking reliable power for lunar bases while scientists warn of safety risks
articles.summary: The US, China, and Russia are competing to deploy nuclear reactors on the Moon to power sustainable lunar bases.

articles.title: From a remote Texas base, SpaceX's launch shows Louisiana what to expect. 'See the future.'
articles.description: SpaceX's Starship — a 40-story, two-stage behemoth, the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown — climbed over the Gulf as hundreds watched. Here’s what the scene was like in Texas as Musk’s Vermilion Parish spaceport begins to come to life.
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship, the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown at 40 stories tall, successfully launched from a Texas base, demonstrating the future of heavy-lift launch capability. The achievement showcases humanity's progress toward ambitious space exploration goals.

articles.title: Is SpaceX's Starship The Most Powerful Rocket Ever Built?
articles.description: SpaceX fitted Starship's first-stage booster with 33 engines, enough to make you wonder how it compares with the most powerful rockets humans have ever built.
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship features 33 engines on its first-stage booster, making it among the most powerful rockets ever constructed. This engineering achievement represents a major milestone in rocket development and deep-space exploration capability.

articles.title: Rocket Report: SpaceX completes launch triple-header; Rocket Lab nets big contract
articles.description:
Welcome to Edition 9.13 of the Rocket Report!
This week, SpaceX celebrated the first orbital launch of its new Starship rocket. I’m not sure many people, at least those outside of SpaceX, expected it to take 14 flights of Starship before it technically reache…
articles.summary: SpaceX completed a triple-header launch series and achieved the first orbital launch of a new Starship variant, while Rocket Lab secured a major contract. The report highlights accelerating progress in commercial spaceflight operations.

articles.title: Strange Galaxy Pattern Has Scientists Wondering If Our Entire Cosmos Could Be Inside A Black Hole
articles.description: The universe may be 13.8 billion years old, but there’s still plenty we don’t understand about the cosmos. A researcher analyzing observations from the James Webb Space Telescope has spotted a puzzling pattern in how distant galaxies rotate. The finding has r…
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered unusual galaxy patterns that prompt exploration of whether our entire universe could exist within a black hole, offering a fascinating new perspective on cosmic structure. This theoretical investigation deepens our understanding of cosmological possibilities.

articles.title: Successful Earth flyby improves Juice’s course to Jupiter
articles.description: The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) skimmed the very outer edge of Earth’s atmosphere on 28 September, using the gravity of our home planet to alter its route to Jupiter using very little fuel.
articles.summary: ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) successfully executed an Earth flyby gravity assist maneuver to refine its trajectory toward Jupiter.

articles.title: A galaxy spinning out of sync
articles.description:
Image:
			
Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It’s one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.
As a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disc of stars, gas and dust. Its centre is dominated by a galactic bulge.
The diffuse off-white glow of the galaxy’s bulge comes from stars smaller, older, and cooler than the massive blue stars that dot the galaxy’s outer disc. These tightly packed stars orbit a supermassive black hole containing millions of times the Sun’s mass. Scientists have found signs that this black hole is actively growing, drawing gas inward with its gravitational pull.
With a flat, starry disc and diffusely glowing centre, NGC 4698 looks a lot like a typical spiral galaxy — but this galaxy is far from normal. NGC 4698 is one of only a few known spiral galaxies with a bulge that extends out from the disc at a right angle. The elongation is faintly visible in this Hubble image, which shows the ghostly glow of the starry bulge peeking above and below the dusty disc. What’s more, the stars and gas nearest the galaxy’s centre rotate perpendicular to the rest of the disc.
What could cause a galaxy to be so out of sync? Astronomers have found that the culprit likely lies outside the galaxy. If NGC 4698 funneled in gas from an outside source, the newly collected gas could have formed a disc of gas and stars in the galaxy’s centre, at an angle relative to the rest of the disc. Some observations suggest that this galaxy once experienced a minor galactic merger, as evidenced by a short ‘tail’ of hydrogen streaming from one side of the galaxy.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#18103; PI: Thilker) focusing on galaxies in the Virgo Cluster.
[Image Description: A spiral galaxy viewed at an angle, with a bright central bulge and winding spiral arms. The arms form a ring around the galaxy, without appearing to reach its centre. Prominent red-brown dust lanes weave through the arms, which are also dotted with bright blue and reddish regions of star formation. The galaxy is set against a dark background scattered with stars and faint distant galaxies.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope captures a spiral galaxy that exhibits unusual rotational dynamics, revealing unexpected complexity in galactic structure.

articles.title: X-Rays and AI Reveal How Spacecraft Heat Shields Burn in Real Time
articles.description: Heat shields are undeniably one of the most important parts of any spacecraft that intends to enter an atmosphere. And the material they are made out of is absolutely critical. Improving them has been a bit of a challenge though, as typically researchers only get “before” and “after” pictures of when the heat shield completes its job of helping a spacecraft land safely back on Earth. That changed recently, though, with a collaboration between NASA and the Advanced Light Source (ALS) located at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, which allowed researchers to watch a heat shield fall apart in real time.
articles.summary: Researchers use X-rays and artificial intelligence to study how spacecraft heat shields perform in real-time during atmospheric entry, advancing spacecraft technology.

articles.title: Asteroid Bennu Has an Identity Crisis, and Jupiter Might Be to Blame
articles.description: Asteroid sample return missions have brought well preserved samples of the early solar system (that hadn’t been roasted in a fireball) back to Earth for the first time. But those samples, like the OSIRIS-REx sample from asteroid (101955) Bennu, sometimes provide more questions than answers. A new paper, published in Science Advances from researchers at ETH Zurich and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, highlights one of those questions - why Bennu appears to have been born in both the inner and outer solar system - and a possible answer to it.
articles.summary: Analysis of asteroid Bennu samples suggests Jupiter's gravitational influence may have altered the asteroid's composition and orbital history in the early solar system.
